analysis.one_liner: Bans excessive and non-performance-based pay for executives at banks bailed out with taxpayer money.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 247-171, but the Senate never voted on it and it died on the Senate calendar when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Banks that took emergency federal capital under the 2008 bailout would have been barred from paying executives unreasonable or excessive compensation, or any bonus not tied to performance standards the Treasury Secretary would write. Firms would have had to report annually how many officers and employees got pay above set thresholds. It also created a commission to study how executive pay connects to company performance.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, whose money was propping up the banks, would gain the strongest say yet over executive pay at firms living on public support. Rank-and-file bank employees and shareholders would also gain from pay tied to firm health rather than deal-chasing.

how_it_helps.text: Bars TARP banks from paying executives compensation that is unreasonable or excessive, or any bonus not directly based on performance measures that include the firm's stability, the individual's performance, and risk-management compliance [S4][S5].

Requires covered firms to report annually how many officers, directors, and employees received compensation above $500,000, $1 million, $2 million, $3 million, and $5 million, with reports posted online by Treasury [S3][S5].

Closes a loophole by blocking otherwise-prohibited bonuses regardless of when the arrangement was signed, and lets Treasury claw back prohibited pay if a firm that promised repayment defaults [S4][S5].

analysis.who_pays: Executives and highly paid employees at banks that took bailout capital, who would face a cap and performance tests on bonuses while their firms' federal money remained outstanding, plus the firms' compliance burden.

drawbacks.text: The restriction applies only while the federal capital is outstanding, so a firm could escape it by repaying Treasury; the strongest objection is that hard pay limits could push out executives and make it harder for weakened banks to recover and pay taxpayers back [S5].

The definition of 'unreasonable or excessive' is left to standards the Treasury Secretary writes within 30 days, so the practical bite depends heavily on the administration carrying it out; firms with TARP investments of $250 million or less can also be exempted [S5].
Compensation reports do not have to name the individuals receiving the large payments, limiting public accountability to head-counts and amounts [S3][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is narrowly aimed at firms living on public money, which is where the taxpayer's interest in executive pay is strongest, and it builds in escape valves for firms that repay Treasury. The main honest cost is that constraining pay at weakened banks could complicate recovery and repayment, but the bill's exemption for repaying firms is designed to answer exactly that objection. The anonymous reporting requirement blunts some of the transparency value, but the pay caps and clawback are real.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a recorded vote of 247-171, but the Senate simply read it and placed it on the calendar and never brought it to a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee ordered the bill reported amended on a 38-22 vote and it was reported on March 30, 2009 [S7].
The House passed the bill by a recorded vote of 247-171 with 1 present on April 1, 2009; 237 of 253 House Democrats voted yes and 10 of 178 House Republicans voted yes [S8].

The Senate received the bill on April 2, 2009, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on April 23, 2009, where it remained without any further action [S7][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives at banks that took bailout capital and the banks themselves are better off, since no binding statutory pay restriction was ever enacted; taxpayers never got the performance-based pay rules the House approved.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 23, 2009 and delivered introductory remarks [S7].

for.name: Rep. Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Moved the bill through committee to a 38-22 report vote in one week and managed floor consideration, including an amendment offered on the floor [S7].

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the House-passed bill to a Senate vote; it sat on the Senate calendar from April 23, 2009 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Executives at TARP recipient banks
against.what_they_did: Opposed binding restrictions on executive pay at bailout recipients while Treasury's own compensation rules were being contested.

sides.party_line_note: In the House, 237 of 253 Democrats voted yes while only 10 of 178 Republicans did, making the 247-171 passage overwhelmingly a Democratic vote; no Senate vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: TARP recipient banks and their executives
industries.note: Firms that took federal bailout capital would have faced pay caps, performance-based bonus tests, annual compensation reporting, and clawbacks on default, but could escape the restrictions by agreeing to repay Treasury. Their interest in avoiding these limits ran against taxpayers funding their rescue.

industries.industry: Banking and financial services industry generally
industries.note: The bill covered only firms that took direct TARP capital; the summary states the prohibition does not apply to institutions that merely did business with a recipient, so most of the industry was untouched. Community banks with TARP investments of $250 million or less could be exempted.
Taxpayers were the source of the bailout capital and stood to gain stronger control over how executives at rescued firms were paid, including performance measures tied to repaying the United States.
